before.public_section:
Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph: $V$ and the edge-label set $E$ are finite, and each $e\in E$ has a singleton or two-element endpoint set $\partial e\subseteq V$. Distinct labels may have the same endpoint set. Let $B\subseteq V$ be a designated boundary set and let $\xi$ be an equivalence relation on $B$; vertices in each $\xi$-class are wired together, while vertices outside $B$ remain separate. For $A\subseteq E$, let $k_\xi(A)$ be the number of connected components, including isolated vertices, after wiring the $\xi$-classes and opening exactly the edges in $A$. A loop does not join distinct vertices.

For $q\in[1,\infty)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK weight of $A$ and its partition function are

$$w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)},\qquad Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}:=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A).$$

The finite FK random-cluster probability is $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)/Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$. Every weight is positive and finite, and the finite sum $Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ is positive and finite. The free boundary condition is the identity partition on $B$; the wired boundary condition identifies all vertices of $B$ in one class.

When $G$ is a finite simple graph with the Potts/FK convention of the earlier finite Potts definition, $\xi$ is free, $q=Q$ is an integer at least two, and every activity equals $v=p/(1-p)$, this definition gives the same normalized FK law, since $w_{FK}(A)=(1-p)^{-|E|}w_{G,p,Q}^{\xi}(A)$.

before.public_section:
Let $E_\infty$ be the nearest-neighbor edge set of $\mathbb Z^2$, and let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$. Let $E_n$ contain the edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $\partial\Lambda_n$ be the vertices of $\Lambda_n$ adjacent to a vertex outside it. Fix $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$. For each boundary partition $\xi_n$ on $\partial\Lambda_n$, let $\phi_{n,p,q}^{\xi_n}$ be the finite FK law of [[def-csm-frontier-fk-real-boundaries]] on $(\Lambda_n,E_n)$ and extend its configurations to $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ by setting all edges outside $E_n$ closed.

An **infinite-volume FK state** at $(p,q)$ is any probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ that is a cylinder-probability limit of such extended finite-volume laws along a sequence $n_j\to\infty$ and boundary partitions $\xi_{n_j}$. Cylinder-probability convergence means convergence of the probability of every assignment on every finite set of edges. When they exist, the **free FK state** and **wired FK state** are the cylinder limits for the identity and one-class partitions, respectively, at every $n$. Their existence and uniqueness as cylinder limits are established by a later A-page lemma. For either state $\phi^b_{p,q}$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, define $\theta^b(p,q):=\phi^b_{p,q}(0\leftrightarrow\infty)$, where $0\leftrightarrow\infty$ means that the open cluster of the origin is not contained in any finite box, and define

$$p_c^b(q):=\inf\{p\in(0,1):\theta^b(p,q)>0\}.$$

No equality of free and wired states at $p=p_c$ is part of this definition.

Let $E_\infty$ be the nearest-neighbor edge set of $\mathbb Z^2$, and let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$. Let $E_n$ contain the edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $\partial\Lambda_n$ be the vertices of $\Lambda_n$ adjacent to a vertex outside it. Fix $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$. For each boundary partition $\xi_n$ on $\partial\Lambda_n$, let $\phi_{n,p,q}^{\xi_n}$ be the finite FK law on $(\Lambda_n,E_n)$ with mass proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_{\xi_n}(A)}$ for $A\subseteq E_n$, where $k_{\xi_n}(A)$ counts components after wiring the partition classes and extend its configurations to $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ by setting all edges outside $E_n$ closed.

An **infinite-volume FK state** at $(p,q)$ is any probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ that is a cylinder-probability limit of such extended finite-volume laws along a sequence $n_j\to\infty$ and boundary partitions $\xi_{n_j}$. Cylinder-probability convergence means convergence of the probability of every assignment on every finite set of edges. When they exist, the **free FK state** and **wired FK state** are the cylinder limits for the identity and one-class partitions, respectively, at every $n$. Their existence and uniqueness as probability-measure cylinder limits are established by a later A-page lemma under its stated measure-extension hypothesis. For either state $\phi^b_{p,q}$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, define $\theta^b(p,q):=\phi^b_{p,q}(0\leftrightarrow\infty)$, where $0\leftrightarrow\infty$ means that the open cluster of the origin is not contained in any finite box, and define

$$p_c^b(q):=\inf\{p\in(0,1):\theta^b(p,q)>0\}.$$

No equality of free and wired states at $p=p_c$ is part of this definition.

before.public_section:
For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

before.public_section:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected plane graph with a fixed embedding and $|V|\geq1$. Use the free partition on all primal vertices, $B=V$. Its plane dual multigraph $G^*$ has one vertex for each face, including the unbounded face, and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; use the identity partition on the dual face-vertices. The unbounded face is one dual vertex, so this convention retains the exterior-face connection in the dual. For a primal open set $A\subseteq E$, let $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, so a dual edge is open exactly when its crossing primal edge is closed. For $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$ define $p^*\in(0,1)$ by

$$\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}=q\frac{1-p}{p}.$$

Then complementing the primal edges sends the finite FK law $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$ to the dual FK law $\phi_{G^*,p^*,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$: the random dual edge set $A^*$ has exactly that distribution. The unnormalized weight ratio is the configuration-independent factor $q^{|V|-1}((1-p)/p^*)^{|E|}$; the exponent $|V|-1$ includes the exterior-face contribution under this identity-partition convention.

before.public_section: For every $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the free finite-volume FK laws on $\Lambda_n$ are stochastically increasing under restriction as $n$ grows, and the wired finite-volume FK laws are stochastically decreasing under restriction. Both sequences therefore have unique cylinder-probability limits, and those limits are probability measures on $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$; hence the free and wired infinite-volume states are well-defined.

current.public_section: For every $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the free finite-volume FK laws on $\Lambda_n$ are stochastically increasing under restriction as $n$ grows, and the wired finite-volume FK laws are stochastically decreasing under restriction. The probabilities of every finite-coordinate atom therefore have unique nonnegative normalized consistent numerical limits. Under Countable Choice, each limiting family extends uniquely to a probability measure on the cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra of $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$. Thus the free and wired infinite-volume states exist under this measure-extension hypothesis.

before.public_section: Let $a,b\geq1$ be integers and let $Q_{a,b}=\{0,\ldots,a\}\times\{0,\ldots,b\}$ have its nearest-neighbor square-grid edges, drawn as unit horizontal and vertical segments. A left-to-right path is a finite edge path whose endpoints lie on the sides $x=0$ and $x=a$; a bottom-to-top path is defined analogously using $y=0$ and $y=b$. Every left-to-right path and every bottom-to-top path in $Q_{a,b}$ share a vertex.

current.public_section: Let $a,b\geq1$ be integers and let $Q_{a,b}=\{0,\ldots,a\}\times\{0,\ldots,b\}$ have its nearest-neighbor square-grid edges, drawn as unit horizontal and vertical segments. A left-to-right path is a finite edge path whose endpoints lie on the sides $x=0$ and $x=a$; a bottom-to-top path is defined analogously using $y=0$ and $y=b$. Every left-to-right path and every bottom-to-top path in $Q_{a,b}$ share a vertex.

Let $n\ge2$ be an integer and let $C\subseteq[0,1]^n$ be coordinatewise increasing and a finite union of axis-parallel boxes, with specified open or closed endpoint conventions. Degenerate boxes are allowed. Let $v_r$ denote elementary $r$-dimensional box volume: a box has the product of its side lengths as volume, and finite unions are evaluated by a common coordinate-endpoint subdivision, with coordinate faces assigned volume zero. Put $f=\mathbf1_C$, $a=v_n(C)$, and

$$F_i=v_{n-1}\{x_{-i}\in[0,1]^{n-1}:f(x_{-i},1)-f(x_{-i},0)=1\},\qquad M=\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i.$$

If $M=0$, then $a(1-a)=0$. If $M>0$, then

$$a(1-a)\le\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^nF_i}{1+\log(1/M)}.$$

In every case,

$$\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i\ge\frac14a(1-a)\frac{\log n}{n}.$$

Logarithms are natural. Endpoint influence uses the actual values on the faces. The assertion and proof use only finite box volumes, finite probability spaces and elementary real calculus; they require no countable product measure or choice principle.

For an integer $m\geq1$, let $T_m$ be the labelled square cellulation obtained by quotienting the unit square cellulation of $\mathbb R^2$ by $m\mathbb Z^2$. Its vertices are $V=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$. For every $(i,j)\in V$, retain a horizontal edge label $h(i,j)$ from $(i,j)$ to $(i+1,j)$, a vertical edge label $v(i,j)$ from $(i,j)$ to $(i,j+1)$, and a square face label $f(i,j)$. All indices are modulo $m$. Distinct labels remain distinct even when their endpoints agree: for $m=2$ this retains parallel edges, and for $m=1$ it retains two loops. In a face boundary retain its four edge occurrences before reducing coefficients modulo two. Thus $|V|=|F|=m^2$ and $|E|=2m^2$. The dual has vertices $f(i,j)$ and a separate label $e^*$ crossing each primal label $e$; specifically $h(i,j)^*$ joins $f(i,j-1)$ to $f(i,j)$ and $v(i,j)^*$ joins $f(i-1,j)$ to $f(i,j)$. Its faces correspond to primal vertices and use the dual square cellulation.

Let $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$ be the field with addition and multiplication modulo two. Let $C_0=\mathbb F_2^V$, $C_1=\mathbb F_2^E$, and $C_2=\mathbb F_2^F$ have the indicated labelled bases. Define $\partial_1:C_1\to C_0$ by summing the two endpoint occurrences of each edge, so a loop has zero boundary, and define $\partial_2:C_2\to C_1$ by

$$\partial_2 f(i,j)=h(i,j)+v(i+1,j)+h(i,j+1)+v(i,j).$$

Then $\partial_1\partial_2=0$ and $H:=\ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2$ has dimension two. For $A\subseteq E$, let $C_1(A)$ be the coordinate subspace generated by its labels, put $Z(A)=C_1(A)\cap\ker\partial_1$, and define

$$r(A):=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{im}\bigl(Z(A)\longrightarrow H\bigr).$$

Let $k(A)$ count all components of the spanning graph $(V,A)$, including isolated vertices. Let $A^*=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, and let $k^*(A^*)$ count all components of this dual spanning graph. Define $r^*(A^*)$ by the same matrix construction on the dual cellulation. Then

$$r(A)\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad k^*(A^*)-1=|A|-|V|+k(A)-r(A),\qquad r^*(A^*)=2-r(A).$$

For every real $q\geq1$, set $p=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. Give both primal and dual graphs the finite FK law with parameter $(p,q)$ and identity boundary partition. Write $w(A)$ and $w^*(A^*)$ for their unnormalized weights, $\phi$ and $\phi^*$ for their laws, and $\nu$ for the image of $\phi$ under $A\mapsto A^*$. Then

$$\frac{w(A)}{w^*(A^*)}=q^{r(A)-1}.$$

For every dual configuration $B\subseteq E^*$, the two partition functions are equal and the exact normalized likelihood is

$$\frac{\nu(B)}{\phi^*(B)}=q^{1-r^*(B)}.$$

In particular this likelihood lies in $[q^{-1},q]$, and hence also in $[q^{-2},q^2]$. For every event $\mathcal E\subseteq2^{E^*}$,

$$q^{-2}\phi^*(\mathcal E)\leq\nu(\mathcal E)\leq q^2\phi^*(\mathcal E).$$

The same event bounds hold after any labelled graph isomorphism identifying the dual torus with the primal torus.

Let $q\geq1$ be a finite real number. On the nearest-neighbor square lattice let $\Lambda_n=\{-n,\ldots,n\}^2$, let $E_n$ consist of edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_\infty=n\}$. For $p\in(0,1)$ and a partition $\xi$ of $B_n$, give $A\subseteq E_n$ probability proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)}$, where $k_\xi$ counts components after the partition classes are identified. Write $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ for the free partition when $b=0$ and the one-class wired partition when $b=1$.

For every event $C$ determined by finitely many edge coordinates, the numerical limits
$$\pi^b_{p,q}(C):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(C),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},$$
exist. They are consistent, nonnegative normalized finite-coordinate probability families, invariant under translations and quarter-turns. On increasing cylinder events they are increasing in $p$, with $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$. Every cylinder-probability limit of arbitrary boundary partitions lies between these two families on increasing cylinder events. There is an at most countable set $D_q\subset(0,1)$ such that $\pi^0_{p,q}(C)=\pi^1_{p,q}(C)$ for every cylinder event $C$ whenever $p\notin D_q$.

Let $D_r$ be the event that actual open edges inside $\Lambda_r$ join $0$ to $B_r$, and define the real numbers
$$\Theta_b(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^b_{p,q}(D_r).$$
Then $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$ for $0<p<p'<1$, and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^1_{n,p,q}(0\leftrightarrow B_n)=\Theta_1(p,q).$$
Connections here use actual edges, not artificial boundary-identification paths. These are statements about real limits and finite probability tables; existence of a countably additive probability on the infinite configuration space is not asserted.

Let $P$ have vertices $(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2$ with $u\equiv v\pmod2$ and straight edges with displacement $(\pm1,\pm1)$. For a positive integer $m$, quotient its labelled cellulation by the periods $(m,m)$ and $(-m,m)$, retaining distinct edge labels even if endpoints agree. Give this torus the finite FK law $\phi$ with identity boundary partition, real $q\geq1$, and $p=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. A closed coordinate rectangle means its induced primal graph on the indicated integer vertices. A horizontal crossing joins its extreme left and right coordinate layers; a vertical crossing joins its extreme bottom and top layers, using only its edges. Paths may be stopped at their first target-layer visit.

Put

$$r(q)=\frac1{1+\sqrt q},\qquad a_0(q)=\frac1{1+q^2},\qquad a(q)=r(q)a_0(q),\qquad b(q)=\frac{a(q)^3}{2(1+q^2)}.$$

For every positive integer $N$ divisible by four and every $m>N$, the closed square $[0,N]^2$ has horizontal and vertical crossing probabilities at least $a(q)$. If additionally $m>3N/2$, the closed rectangle $[0,3N/2]\times[0,N]$ has horizontal crossing probability at least $b(q)$, and the corresponding vertical crossing bound holds for $[0,N]\times[0,3N/2]$. The same bounds hold after every translation by a vertex of $P$. Every rectangle in these conclusions embeds in the torus under its stated size condition. No restriction on $q$ beyond real $q\geq1$ is imposed.

before.public_section: For each $q\geq1$ and aspect ratio $\alpha>1$, there is a constant $c(\alpha,q)>0$ such that the following holds. Let $n,m$ be positive integers with $m>\lceil\alpha n\rceil$, let $T_m=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$ with its nearest-neighbor horizontal and vertical edges and periodic boundary conditions, and give its edges the FK law with no boundary wiring, parameter $q$, and $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. The probability of a horizontal open crossing of the vertex rectangle $\{0,\ldots,\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\}\times\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is at least $c(\alpha,q)$, uniformly in $n$ and $m$.

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph, let $B\subseteq V$ have boundary partition $\xi$, fix $q\geq1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$, and let $\phi=\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ be the finite FK law. For every increasing event $A\subseteq2^E$ with $0<\phi(A)<1$ and $|E|\geq2$, define the conditional influence of edge $e$ by

$$I_A(e):=\phi(A\mid \omega_e=1)-\phi(A\mid\omega_e=0).$$

There is a constant $c(q,\varepsilon)>0$ such that

$$\max_{e\in E}I_A(e)\geq c(q,\varepsilon)\,\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\frac{\log|E|}{|E|}.$$

Let $q\geq1$ be real, $p\in(0,1)$, $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, and $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ the finite square-lattice FK law with free boundary partition $b=0$ or wired partition $b=1$. All paths below use actual open lattice edges, not artificial wiring edges. For each cylinder event $A$ let $\pi^b_{p,q}(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(A)$ be its numerical cylinder limit. Put $p_s=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $D_r$ be the cylinder event that $0$ connects inside $\Lambda_r$ to its vertex boundary. Then $a_n(p,q)=\phi^1_{n,p,q}(D_n)$ decreases, and
$$\Theta^1(p,q):=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r).$$
For $p>p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)>0$; for $p<p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)=0$. Consequently $\inf\{p\in(0,1):\Theta^1(p,q)>0\}=p_s$. No value at $p_s$ is asserted. These numerical conclusions do not require Countable Choice or the extension of cylinder weights to an infinite-volume measure.

More precisely, fix $p>p_s$ and any real $\alpha>1$. Put $r_k=\lfloor\alpha^k\rfloor$. For all sufficiently large $k$, let $A_k$ be the cylinder event that an actual open simple circuit surrounds $\Lambda_{r_k}$, lies outside $\Lambda_{r_k}$ and strictly inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$, and is connected inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$ to its vertex boundary. There are $C,\varepsilon>0$ and an integer $K$ such that $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}<1/2$ for $k\geq K$ and, for every $n\geq m\geq N\geq K$,
$$\phi^1_{r_{n+2},p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq\prod_{k=N}^{n}(1-d_k),\qquad \pi^1_{p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq1-\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}d_k.$$
For $0<p<t<1$ and $H_n$ the finite Hamming distance to $D_n$, the finite cylinder expectation satisfies
$$\pi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{t,q}}H_n\}.$$
For every $0<s<p_s$ and every $d>0$, there are $C_d,n_d$ such that $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq C_d n^{-(2d+4)}$ for $n\geq n_d$. The expectation here is a finite sum of cylinder atom weights.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a given probability space. For each $y\in\mathbb Z^2$, let $S_y$ be a measurable random finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $y$, with the discrete sigma-algebra on the countable collection of such sets. Assume the sets $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed and that $\mathbb E|S_0|^r<\infty$ for every real $r>0$. A lattice animal is a finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $0$. Define the extended measurable envelope
$$M_z=\sup\{|S_y|:y\in\mathbb Z^2,\ z\in S_y\}.$$
Almost surely every $M_z$ is a finite maximum, and there is a deterministic finite constant $K_0$ such that, almost surely, every sufficiently large lattice animal $\Gamma$ satisfies
$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|.$$
More generally, for any given independent identically distributed field $X_y\geq1$ with finite moments of every positive order, there is a deterministic finite $K$ such that almost surely $\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq K|\Gamma|$ for every sufficiently large lattice animal. The random cutoff may depend on the realization. This result assumes the stated random family on a probability space; it does not construct an infinite product law or require a choice axiom to supply that law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every real $q\geq1$ and $0<p<\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$, the square-lattice wired FK cluster $C_x$ has $\mathbb E|C_x|^d<\infty$ for every real $d>0$. There are constants $C(p,q),c(p,q)>0$ such that every probability measure $\phi$ obtained as a cylinder limit of finite-volume FK laws on boxes with arbitrary boundary partitions satisfies
$$\phi(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z^2).$$
Here $x\leftrightarrow y$ means connection by a finite path of actual open lattice edges. In particular every such state has zero probability of an infinite cluster at a given vertex. The constants are uniform over all these cylinder-limit states at the fixed $(p,q)$. No conclusion at the self-dual parameter or equality of the critical free and wired measures is asserted. Countable Choice is used for probability-law extension and selection of countably many coupling kernels in this proof; it is not a premise of the separate numerical finite-volume threshold theorem.

Let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, $J>0$, and $\beta>0$. On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n\}$ and let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$. The $Q$-state Potts model has spins $\sigma:\Lambda_n\to\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, fixed plus boundary $\sigma|_{B_n}=1$, and finite-volume Gibbs probabilities proportional to $e^{-\beta H_n(\sigma)}$, where
$$H_n(\sigma)=-J\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}.$$
Define its plus-boundary order parameter by
$$m_Q^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^+(\sigma_0=1)-Q^{-1},$$
when the limit exists, and define $\beta_c:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_Q^+(\beta)>0\}$. Then the limit exists and
$$\beta_c J=\log(1+\sqrt Q).$$
The assertion is conditional on the FK exact-threshold input in [[thm-csm-frontier-fk-square-critical-point]] and the current finite Potts/FK interfaces identified below.

used_external_supplier_bindings.public_section:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

A **finite undirected multigraph** consists of a finite vertex set $V$, a finite
edge set $M$, and an endpoint map assigning to each $e\in M$ either a singleton
$\{v\}$ or a two-element subset $\{u,v\}$ of $V$. An edge assigned $\{v\}$ is a
**loop** at $v$. Distinct members of $M$ assigned the same endpoint set are
**parallel edges**.

A **finite directed graph**, or **digraph**, consists of a finite vertex set $V$
and a set $A\subseteq V\times V$ of **arcs**. An arc $(u,v)$ is directed from
$u$ to $v$; an arc $(v,v)$ is a directed loop.

These objects are variants, not instances of the default graph convention in
[[def-finite-simple-graph]] and [[rem-finite-simple-graph-convention]]. A theorem
stated merely for a graph therefore neither permits loops or parallel edges nor
supplies directions to its edges.

A **plane graph** is a finite simple graph ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]) together with distinct points of $\mathbb R^2$ for its vertices and a polygonal arc ([[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]]) for each edge, joining its endpoints, such that an edge interior contains no vertex and two edge arcs meet only at a common endpoint. A finite simple graph is **planar** if it is isomorphic to the abstract graph underlying some plane graph.

A **face** is a region of the complement of the drawing ([[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]). The **boundary subgraph** of a face consists of the vertices and whole edges lying in its frontier; this is a subgraph in the sense of [[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]].

For a connected plane graph, walking once around a face with that face locally on the same side gives its **facial boundary walk**. Its **length** is the number of edge traversals, not the number of distinct edges: an edge incident with the same face on both local sides is traversed twice. For a disconnected plane graph a face may have several boundary walks; its boundary length is the sum of their lengths. No boundary walk is assumed to be a cycle unless a later connectivity result proves it.

Let $G$ be a connected plane graph with face set $F(G)$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]). Its **dual multigraph** $G^*$ has vertex set $F(G)$ and one edge $e^*$ for every primal edge $e$. If the two local sides of $e$ belong to faces $f$ and $g$, then $e^*$ has endpoints $f,g$.

By [[lem-plane-edge-face-incidence]], a bridge has the same face on both local sides, so its dual edge is a loop. Different primal edges may have the same incident face pair, so their duals may be parallel. These are permitted by [[def-multigraph-loop-and-digraph]]. The definition is attached to the fixed plane embedding: different embeddings of the same abstract planar graph may have nonisomorphic dual multigraphs.

If a plane graph has $c$ connected components, then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=1+c.$$

This includes the null graph, for which $c=0$ and the complement is its single face. Component sets and their finite cardinalities are those of [[cor-connected-components-partition-the-vertex-set]] and [[def-finite-cardinality]], and face finiteness is [[lem-plane-graph-faces-are-finite-with-one-unbounded-face]].

In a plane graph ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), if the relative interior of an edge meets the frontier of a face, then the whole edge lies in that frontier. An edge on a cycle is incident with two distinct faces, one on each local side. A bridge is incident with one face on both local sides and is therefore traversed twice in that face's boundary walk. Edge deletion is as in [[def-graph-deletion-contraction-minor-and-subdivision]], and the bridge cases use the arc-complement fact [[lem-polygonal-arc-does-not-separate-the-plane]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $A$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$. Fix a bijection $(i_n)_{n\geq1}:\mathbb N_{>0}	o\mathbb Z^d$ and give $X$ the metric
$$d_X(\sigma,\eta)=\sum_{n\geq1}2^{-n}\mathbf 1_{\{\sigma_{i_n}
e\eta_{i_n}\}}.$$
For a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and $B\subseteq A^F$, write $[F,B]=\{\sigma\in X:\sigma|_F\in B\}$ and let $\mathcal C=\{[F,B]:F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite},\ B\subseteq A^F\}$ be the cylinder algebra. A family $(
u_F)_{F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite}}$ of probability measures on $A^F$ is **consistent** if $(\pi_E^F)_*
u_F=
u_E$ whenever $E\subseteq F$, where $\pi_E^F:A^F	o A^E$ is restriction. Such a family defines $\mu_0([F,B])=
u_F(B)$; consistency makes this a well-defined normalized finitely additive probability on $\mathcal C$. Then $X$ is compact, the Borel sigma-algebra is $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, and $\mu_0$ extends uniquely to a probability on $\sigma(\mathcal C)$. Moreover, every sequence of probabilities on this sigma-algebra has a subsequence whose cylinder probabilities converge to those of a probability measure; along that subsequence integrals of every continuous $f:X	o\mathbb R$ converge.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, and let each edge activity $v_e$ be finite and nonnegative. Use the Potts weight $w_P(\sigma)=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}}(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}})$ and FK weight $w_{FK}(A)=Q^{k_G(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e$ from the finite definitions. Define
$$W(\sigma,A):=\prod_{e\notin A}1\prod_{e\in A}v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}},\qquad (\sigma,A)\in[Q]^V\times2^E.$$
The normalized joint law $\nu(\sigma,A):=W(\sigma,A)/\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$ has Potts marginal $w_P/Z_P$ and FK marginal $w_{FK}/Z_{FK}$, with $Z_P=Z_{FK}=\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$. Conditional on an edge set $A$ of positive probability, the colors of its connected components are independent and uniform on $[Q]$. Thus for every $x,y\in V$,
$$\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=\frac1Q+\left(1-\frac1Q\right)\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y),$$
where $x\leftrightarrow y$ means that $x$ and $y$ lie in the same component of $G_A$.
